extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent owners, and patent challengers (PTAB/IPR practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and summary of USPTO changes (Director institution policy and Proposed Rules) governing institution of IPR/PGR proceedings and limits on parallel/serial challenges; practical takeaways for patentees and petitioners on strategy and procedure before the PTAB.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director authority to institute IPRs/PGRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective October 20, 2025, the USPTO Director will decide whether to institute IPR and post-grant review (PGR) trials (in consultation with at least three PTAB judges). This replaces prior practice where merits panels of APJs made institution decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director will consider both discretionary denial and merits issues raised by the petition; may issue a 'summary notice' granting or denying institution; may issue fuller decisions for "novel or important factual or legal issues"; may refer institution decisions to one or more PTAB members for detailed treatment of issues (e.g., claim construction, priority analyses, real-party-in-interest determinations). Petitions referred to an APJ panel prior to Oct. 20, 2025, are unaffected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goals for centralizing institution with Director
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director articulated four goals for the change: (1) eliminate appearance of self-interest; (2) remove perceived referral-signal bias by centralizing decision with the Director; (3) enhance transparency and public trust; and (4) realign duties and responsibilities to the Senate-confirmed Director.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change is asserted to align with 35 U.S.C. § 314(a), which vests authority to institute IPRs/PGRs in the USPTO Director. Centralization may reduce perceived incentives tied to APJ docketing and resource allocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of summary notices for institution decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director will issue 'summary notices' granting or denying institution instead of the typically lengthy analyses previously authored by APJs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary notices may provide only limited guidance, reducing information on why a petition was granted or denied and how APJs view key legal/factual issues, which could limit parties' insight into institution reasoning and strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed bar: no IPRs against patents that survived prior invalidity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposed Rules would prohibit instituting IPRs against patents that have previously survived an invalidity challenge in any forum (including final written decisions in IPR/PGR, ex parte reexaminations, district court, or ITC), or where a pending proceeding will reach a decision on validity before the Final Written Decision would be due.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a substantial shift from current practice where parallel or prior proceedings are one factor in discretionary denial but not an absolute bar. If implemented, only the first instituted petition against a given patent could proceed in many multi-party/serial scenarios, incentivizing early filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed requirement to waive §§102/103 positions in parallel proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rules would require IPR petitioners to stipulate they will not pursue any anticipation (§102) or obviousness (§103) arguments in any other venue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a 'super-Sotera' stipulation: it would foreclose use of anticipation/obviousness arguments in parallel district-court litigation even if those arguments rely on system prior art or other evidence not permissible in IPR. Petitioners could still assert defenses/invalidity under §§101 and 112 and unenforceability in other forums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary-circumstances exception to the bar
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rules create a limited exception allowing an otherwise-barred petition to proceed if the petitioner establishes 'extraordinary circumstances [which] warrant institution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rules clarify that 'extraordinary circumstances' are intended to be very limited and explicitly would not include 'new or additional prior art, new expert testimony, new caselaw . . . new legal argument, or a prior challenger's failure to appeal.' The rule warns that frivolous claims of extraordinary circumstances may result in sanctions, including attorneys' fees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for frivolous extraordinary-circumstances claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Affected petitions that frivolously claim 'extraordinary circumstances' may result in the petitioner being sanctioned, including with attorneys' fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rules caution that invoking the extraordinary-circumstances exception without a proper basis could lead to fee-shifting or other sanctions, deterring misuse of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of current Sotera stipulations (background practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under current practice, petitioners may enter Sotera stipulations promising not to raise in parallel district-court proceedings invalidity grounds that could be raised in IPR (patents and printed publications), while still being able to assert other invalidity grounds (e.g., physical products) in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Proposed Rules would go beyond Sotera stipulations by broadly requiring waivers of §§102/103 across venues, thereby limiting petitioners' ability to preserve certain parallel-challenge strategies that Sotera previously permitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed Rules apply only to IPRs (not PGR or ex parte reexamination)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Proposed Rules would affect only IPR proceedings; they would not extend to post-grant review (PGR) trials or ex parte reexaminations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a result, parties may favor PGRs (especially for newly-granted patents) or ex parte reexamination where appropriate; Director Squires and Acting Director Stewart have favored PGRs over IPR in policy statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier 2024 Notice (withdrawn) on serial petitions and expanded briefing
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO withdrew a 2024 Notice that would have given APJ merits panels discretion to decline to institute 'serial petitions' narrowly defined as petitions filed by the same party (or real party in interest) challenging the same claims, and that would have implemented expanded briefing for discretionary-denial issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The withdrawal signals a shift from an APJ-panel-centric approach to institution toward Director control; the 2024 Notice contained narrower, panel-discretion-focused proposals (including 325(d) considerations) that the new Proposed Rules supersede or replace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded discretionary-denial factors including 'settled expectations'
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO has expanded use of discretionary denials and introduced new factors like 'settled expectations,' including the age of the patent, as considerations supporting denial of institution even where a petition might otherwise be meritorious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Director Review decisions have employed such factors (e.g., reversing a Final Written Decision and terminating proceedings), indicating a broader posture toward limiting institution beyond the formal Proposed Rules; petitioners should account for these discretionary considerations in strategy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical consequences for petition drafting and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Because IPR petitions are limited by word count and the Proposed Rules would preclude raising anticipation/obviousness arguments in parallel forums, challengers must weigh whether filing an IPR is the viable invalidity strategy and may be incentivized to file earliest to preserve PTAB access.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If petitioners lose the race to the PTAB (or are barred by the Proposed Rules), their alternatives include district-court challenges (higher burden: clear and convincing evidence) or ex parte reexamination (non-adversarial, inability to participate post-filing). The Proposed Rules thus materially affect litigation strategy and resource allocation.
